title: Palomino
description: Also called Palomino Fino and Listán Blanco. A neutral grape transformed by flor and the solera into Sherry.
L: Palomino, or Palomino Fino, is a white grape with low acidity, low sugar and neutral flavours: a little apple, almond and salt. As a table wine, it's simple and soft. But as a base for Sherry, its neutrality is perfect: flor yeast, oxygen and the solera write the flavour onto it.

Sherry's flavours come from how it's aged, not from the grape. A strongly aromatic grape would compete with flor's bready, saline notes or with the nutty notes of oxidation. Palomino's low sugar means base wines at 11 to 12.5% alcohol, easy to fortify to the levels needed for each style.
Why is Palomino's neutrality an advantage for Sherry?
Ageing, not the grape, creates Sherry's flavours
Flor and oxidation create the flavours; a neutral grape lets them show.

As an unfortified table wine, Palomino is pale, soft and neutral. In Sherry, its flavour is hidden under flor's bread, almond and salt in Fino, or the walnut and caramel of Oloroso. Palomino's real identity is the Sherry family.
Palomino is a highly aromatic grape.
Not true. It's very neutral, which is why it suits Sherry.
Palomino is neutral, low in acidity and sugar
Sherry's flavours come from ageing, not the grape
Its base wines are easy to fortify
Name other places that grow it

Palomino is about 95% of the vineyards of Jerez, in Andalusia, around Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Sherry triangle. The climate is hot, with over 300 sunny days a year, and two winds: the humid Poniente from the Atlantic and the hot, dry Levante from the east.

The best vineyards are on albariza, a brilliant white soil with up to 40% chalk, formed from marine diatoms. It absorbs winter rain like a sponge and holds it for the dry summer, then forms a hard crust that reduces evaporation. Its white surface reflects sunlight. Pagos, named vineyard areas, like Macharnudo and Carrascal, sit on albariza.
Jerez has its own vocabulary of land and wind.

Palomino is also grown in the Canary Islands, as Listán Blanco, where it makes dry table wines on volcanic soil. Galicia, South Africa, Australia and California grow some, once for fortified wines. Today, a few Jerez producers make unfortified Palomino table wines, showing the albariza in a new way.
What is special about albariza soil?
It stores winter rain for summer
Its chalky structure holds water deep for the dry summer.
Albariza stores water and reflects sun
It's Listán Blanco in the Canaries

After fermentation, base wines are classified. The most delicate are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and put into barrels left about five-sixths full. A layer of yeast called flor grows on the surface, protecting the wine from oxygen and feeding on alcohol and glycerol. It adds bready, almond, saline aromas, from acetaldehyde.

Sherry ages in a solera: tiers of barrels of different ages. Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest tier, the solera, which is refilled from the next oldest, the first criadera, and so on. New wine enters the youngest. By law, no more than 40% can be drawn per year. The blend stays consistent and gains average age.
Old tier drawn, refilled from younger
Why are Sherry barrels left partly empty?
To give flor air to grow on the surface
Flor needs air at the surface to live.

Wines chosen for oxidative ageing are fortified to about 17%. At that strength flor can't survive, so oxygen ages the wine, giving nutty, darker Oloroso. The classification and fortification level decide whether a wine follows the biological path, under flor, or the oxidative one.
Put the solera's movements in order, starting with bottling.
Draw wine from the oldest tier
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill the first criadera from the second
Add new wine to the youngest tier
Each tier passes wine to the older tier.
Flor grows on wines fortified to about 15%, protecting them
The solera blends wines of many ages
At 17% flor dies and the wine ages oxidatively

Fino ages under flor, giving pale, bone-dry wines with almond, bread and salt, at about 15%. Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where cooler, humid sea air keeps flor thick, adding a saline, chamomile freshness. Both are best fresh, soon after bottling.

Oloroso, fortified to 17%, ages with oxygen, turning amber-brown with walnut, toffee and spice, yet dry. Amontillado starts as Fino, then loses its flor and ages oxidatively, combining both styles. Palo Cortado is rare: it loses flor early, giving Amontillado's aroma with Oloroso's body. Cream Sherry is sweetened, often with Pedro Ximénez.
Match each Sherry to its ageing.
The path of ageing defines the style.
An opened bottle of Fino or Manzanilla behaves like a white wine: keep it in the fridge and finish it within a week.
Which Sherry styles are naturally dry?
Fino and Manzanilla age under flor, pale and dry
Oloroso ages oxidatively, dark yet dry
Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine both paths
Pair each Sherry style with food

Fino and Manzanilla suit tapas: olives, almonds, jamón, fried fish, prawns and anchovies. Amontillado suits soups, mushrooms, artichokes and asparagus, notoriously hard to pair. Oloroso suits game, stews and hard cheese. Sweet Pedro Ximénez is poured over vanilla ice cream.

Serve Fino and Manzanilla well chilled, 6 to 8 degrees, in a white wine glass, not a tiny copita. Amontillado at 12 to 14, Oloroso at 14 to 16. Fino and Manzanilla fade within a week once open; Oloroso lasts weeks. En rama Sherry, lightly filtered, is bottled for fresh drinking.
Which Sherry is the classic match for jamón and olives?
Dry, saline Fino and Manzanilla suit salty tapas.
Amontillado is one of the few wines that handles asparagus and artichokes. Its nutty, savoury character doesn't clash with their bitter compounds.
Fino should be served at room temperature.
Not true. Fino and Manzanilla are best well chilled, at 6 to 8 degrees.
Fino suits tapas; Amontillado tricky vegetables; Oloroso game
